newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin defends Chechen policy on eve of debate.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin defends Chechen policy on eve of debate.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, under fire for agreeing to withdraw Russia's last two army units from breakaway Chechnya, on Thursday defended his right as Russia's commander-in-chief to decide on troop movements.

Deputies have condemned the weekend decision as a concession too far to the Chechen rebels and say it threatens Russian territorial integrity. The State Duma lower house of parliament will discuss the move at an extraordinary session on Friday.
"The president is the supreme military commander and is fully entitled to take decisions on the stationing and restationing of troops," his press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.

In an apparent bid to calm deputies' fears, Yeltsin sent a letter to the Duma's communist speaker, Gennady Seleznyov, telling him that he as president was ultimately responsible for safeguarding Russia's territorial integrity.

Yastrzhembsky also said Yeltsin had asked Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the secretary of the Security Council, Ivan Rybkin, to provide a written account to deputies of all recently signed documents concerning the Chechen peace process.

The president, who is recovering from heart surgery at a sanatorium near Moscow, wants to win parliamentary support for the fragile peace process in Chechnya, even though the Duma has little power to dictate government policy.
His critics say the decision to withdraw Russia's last two units from Chechnya means he is effectively sanctioning Chechen demands for independence.

An August peace accord, which halted 21 months of bloody fighting, deferred a final decision on the region's political status for five years, but Chechen rebels regard the deal as Moscow's way of pulling out without losing too much face.
Some deputies have threatened to try to impeach Yeltsin in Friday's debate, though this would be a long drawn-out procedure that has virtually no chance of success.
Yeltsin's Chechen policy won strong support on Thursday from Grigory Yavlinsky, leader of the Duma's liberal Yabloko faction.
"We are categorically against any debates on the impeachment of the president and the sacking of the government...and we support the decisions taken on Chechnya," he told reporters.
"We think there is no reason to convene the extraordinary Duma session and believe the factions that have backed the war since it began in 1994 are just working up hysteria," he said.
Tens of thousands of people, mainly civilians, have been killed in Chechnya since Yeltsin sent troops to crush the region's independence bid in December 1994.
The troops are due to start their withdrawal soon and complete it by January 25, two days before presidential and parliamentary elections in the war-shattered region.
The election campaign began in Chechnya on Wednesday.

Among declared candidates for the presidency are separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and Shamil Basayev, branded by the Kremlin as a terrorist after he led a raid in its southern town of Budennovsk last year in which many people were killed.
A third possible candidate is the rebel Chechen Prime Minister Aslan Maskhadov, though he has so far shown loyalty to Yandarbiyev in order to avoid a split in separatist ranks.
Russian newspapers on Thursday speculated that Moscow would try to exploit differences between rival candidates to increase its influence over a region it failed to subdue by brute force.
"The predicted breakup of the political forces (held together during the war by anti-Russian sentiment) should please the Russian leadership," said the liberal daily Sevodnya.
"The absence of a single candidate among the protagonists of Chechen independence and a struggle between them for the leadership is what the federal forces dreamt of throughout the war," it said.
